add_eyes.name: John Thelwall
add_eyes.role: Radical lecturer and poet, aged 33; acquitted of high treason in 1794 and driven from public lecturing by 1796
add_eyes.where: Walking tour from London to Nether Stowey and Alfoxden, July 1797
add_eyes.vantage_label: the radical guest whose visit drew the spy
add_eyes.authenticity: His 'Pedestrian Excursion' appeared in the Monthly Magazine (1798–1801) and his poems in Poems Chiefly Written in Retirement (1801); modern texts in the Pickering and Chatto Selected Political Writings (2009). His letter to his wife from Alfoxden is known through biographers (Holmes, Roe); its exact date is not checked here.
add_eyes.bio: Thelwall was the most notorious English radical still at liberty, and Coleridge had corresponded with him since 1796. His July 1797 visit, walking from London, brought him into the Alfoxden circle just as the Home Office was being told about strange visitors. He hoped to settle nearby; Coleridge and Poole had to tell him the neighbourhood would not stand it.

sources.title: N. Roe, 'John Thelwall and the West Country: The Road to Nether Stowey Revisited' (Romantic Circles Praxis)
Friends of Coleridge: Coleridge, Thelwall and the 1797 visit

add_eyes.name: Sara Hutchinson
add_eyes.role: Mary Hutchinson's younger sister, aged 24–27; keeping house for her brothers at Sockburn and later Gallow Hill
add_eyes.side: The Hutchinson family; from 1802 Wordsworth's sister-in-law
add_eyes.where: Sockburn-on-Tees (1799); Gallow Hill near Brompton, Yorkshire (1802)
add_eyes.vantage_label: the woman the poems were written to
add_eyes.form: dated letters (mostly later); her 1802 part survives chiefly in others' letters and journals
add_eyes.authenticity: The Letters of Sara Hutchinson from 1800 to 1835, ed. Kathleen Coburn (1954), print her surviving correspondence, which is thin for 1800–02. Her criticism of the leech-gatherer poem is lost and known from the Wordsworths' replies; her presence on the wedding day is recorded in Dorothy's journal. Modern publication, so no quotation.
add_eyes.bio: Coleridge fell in love with her at Sockburn in 1799, and the verse letter of 4 April 1802 that became 'Dejection' was addressed to her. She was also a sharp reader: her complaint that the leech-gatherer poem was tedious made Wordsworth defend and then revise it. Her own voice for these years is faint in the record, and much of it reaches us through what others wrote to her or about her.

add_eyes.name: Francis Jeffrey
add_eyes.role: Edinburgh advocate, aged 29; leading spirit and soon editor of the new Edinburgh Review
add_eyes.authenticity: The review of Southey's Thalaba opens the first number of the Edinburgh Review (vol. 1, no. 1, dated October 1802). It was unsigned, but Jeffrey's authorship is well established.
add_eyes.bio: Jeffrey used a review of Southey's Thalaba to attack the whole group he saw behind it, whose doctrines he found in the Preface to Lyrical Ballads. That review, published the month of the wedding and of 'Dejection', began the long Edinburgh campaign against what would be called the Lake School. It carries the chapter's 'judged' strand beyond Southey's own 1798 notice.

add_entries.headline: A radical walks in from London
add_entries.digest: Having set out from London on 29 June, Thelwall reached Stowey in mid-July and was taken to Alfoxden. He wrote to his wife of the company and the country around the house, and of long talks with Coleridge and Wordsworth by the brook. He found the place so congenial that he began to think of settling nearby.
add_entries.source_note: Departure date from Roe, Romantic Circles Praxis; the letter to Stella Thelwall from Alfoxden is cited by Holmes (Coleridge: Early Visions) and Roe; the day is not checked here.

add_entries.headline: Lines written on the road away
add_entries.digest: Leaving Stowey, Thelwall wrote 'Lines Written at Bridgwater', which looks back on the visit and imagines a retired life near his new friends, far from politics. It is a poem written within days of the Alfoxden talks, by the man whose name filled the spy's reports.
add_entries.source_note: Date of the poem as given by the Friends of Coleridge study of Thelwall's visit; printed in Thelwall, Poems Chiefly Written in Retirement (1801).

add_entries.headline: Telling Thelwall not to come and live here
add_entries.digest: Coleridge wrote to Thelwall that he could not encourage him to settle at Stowey: the village was already in an uproar over the strangers at Alfoxden, and Thelwall's presence would bring real trouble on Poole and the Wordsworths. The letter is the friends' side of the same weeks in which Walsh was reporting to London.
add_entries.source_note: Coleridge to Thelwall, August 1797 (Collected Letters, ed. Griggs, vol. I); day not checked.

add_entries.headline: A letter to Thelwall on the littleness of things
add_entries.digest: Coleridge told Thelwall that he could at times feel the beauty of the landscape deeply, but that more often everything seemed small, and his mind longed for something vast and whole. He wished he could float, like a Hindu god, on an endless ocean. Weeks later he began the Ancient Mariner.
add_entries.source_note: Coleridge to Thelwall, 14 October 1797 (Collected Letters, ed. Griggs, vol. I); date as usually cited, not checked here.

add_entries.headline: Sara finds the leech-gatherer poem dull
add_entries.digest: Sara wrote to Grasmere that the new poem about the old leech-gatherer was tedious and that the old man's long speech dragged. The letter itself is lost; its substance is known because William and Dorothy answered it on 14 June. Her objection led to the heavy revision that became 'Resolution and Independence'.
add_entries.source_note: Lost letter, known from W. and D. Wordsworth to Mary and Sara Hutchinson, 14 June 1802 (Letters, Early Years, ed. de Selincourt, rev. Shaver).

add_entries.headline: She brings Dorothy word that the bridal party is coming
add_entries.digest: Sara stayed at the house while her sister was married at Brompton church. It was she who came to Dorothy, lying on her bed after the news that the service was over, to say the party was on its way back. On the same morning 'Dejection', the public form of the verse letter Coleridge had addressed to her, appeared in the Morning Post without her name.
add_entries.source_note: Dorothy Wordsworth's Grasmere journal, 4 October 1802 (Woof, The Grasmere Journals, 1991); Morning Post, 4 October 1802.

add_entries.headline: The new Edinburgh Review opens fire on a 'sect'
add_entries.digest: The first number of the Edinburgh Review opened with Jeffrey's long notice of Southey's Thalaba. He used it to attack a school of poets who, he said, scorned established rules, cultivated simplicity and low subjects, and took their creed from the Preface to Lyrical Ballads. Wordsworth was not reviewed, but he was plainly a target.
add_entries.quote: belongs to a sect of poets
add_entries.source_note: Edinburgh Review, vol. 1, no. 1 (October 1802), review of Thalaba, opening article.

add_entries.place: Scafell, Eskdale and the western fells
add_entries.headline: The circumcursion, in the notebook
add_entries.digest: Alongside the letters to Sara, Coleridge kept pocket-notebook entries on his solo walk through the western fells: routes, distances, the shapes of crags and becks, and the descent of Broad Stand. They are the working record, written on the move, that the letters later polish.
add_entries.source_note: Notebooks of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, ed. Kathleen Coburn, vol. I (1957), entries for August 1802; days not checked individually.

add_convergences.label: Thelwall at Alfoxden
add_convergences.note: For Thelwall it was a refuge among friends; for Coleridge and Poole it brought a famous radical into a village already watching them; for the Home Office it confirmed that the strangers were radicals. The visit and the spy's arrival are a month apart.

add_convergences.label: Sara's objection and the poet's defence
add_convergences.note: The only reader whose criticism visibly changed a poem of 1802 was a young woman in Yorkshire. Her letter is lost; the replies from William and Dorothy survive, and the poem was rewritten.

add_ties.note: Correspondents since 1796, they met in July 1797 when Thelwall walked to Stowey; Coleridge then had to talk him out of settling there.
Walsh's reports linked the Alfoxden household to Thelwall, the radical acquitted of treason in 1794.
The verse letter of 4 April 1802 was addressed to her; 'Dejection' printed it without her name on her sister's wedding day.
Jeffrey's first Edinburgh Review article attacked Southey's Thalaba, and through it the whole group of poets.

add_claims.claim: 'Lines Written at Bridgwater' composed after the Stowey visit
add_claims.evidence: Date of the poem as printed in Thelwall's Poems Chiefly Written in Retirement (1801)

add_claims.claim: Sara Hutchinson's criticism of 'The Leech Gatherer', answered on 14 June, prompts its revision
add_claims.evidence: W. and D. Wordsworth to Mary and Sara Hutchinson, 14 June 1802 (her letter lost)

add_claims.claim: Jeffrey's Thalaba review in the first Edinburgh Review attacks the new 'sect' of poets

add_threads_out.note: Thelwall was tried for high treason in London in 1794 with Thomas Hardy and John Horne Tooke for his part in the reform societies inspired by the French Revolution; his acquittal and continued notoriety are why his July 1797 visit made Alfoxden look like a nest of conspirators.

updates.why: Walsh's reports name Thelwall's recent visit (entry 3); Thelwall now has entries for July 1797.

fix.note: Dorothy's entry is the only intimate record of the day, and Sara is in it, bringing word that the party was returning; Coleridge's 'Dejection', the public form of his verse letter to Sara, appeared in print the same morning. The same month the first Edinburgh Review opened its attack on the new poets. None of these writers comments on the others.
